concept: Given an array of non-negative integers representing bar heights in a histogram where each bar has a width of one, find the area of the largest rectangle that can be formed within the histogram.

solutions.label: Brute Force
solutions.summary: For every pair of bars, find the minimum height between them and compute the area. Track the maximum area found.

solutions.label: Monotonic Stack
solutions.summary: Use an increasing monotonic stack to efficiently find, for each bar, how far left and right it can extend as the shortest bar in a rectangle.

sections.title: Understanding the Problem
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    subgraph Histogram["Histogram: heights = 2, 1, 5, 6, 2, 3"]
        B1["Bar 0\nH=2"]:::red
        B2["Bar 1\nH=1"]:::red
        B3["Bar 2\nH=5"]:::red
        B4["Bar 3\nH=6"]:::red
        B5["Bar 4\nH=2"]:::red
        B6["Bar 5\nH=3"]:::red
    end
    Q["Question: What is the largest rectangle area?"]:::red
    Histogram --> Q
    classDef red fill:#f87171,color:#000

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Here's the problem. You're given an array of integers representing bar heights in a histogram. Each bar has a width of one. Your task is to find the area of the largest rectangle that fits entirely within the histogram. For example, given heights two, one, five, six, two, three, what's the largest rectangle you can form?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Got it. So I need to find a contiguous group of bars and pick a height no taller than the shortest bar in that group, then maximize width times height. A few questions: Can heights be zero? And what should I return for an empty array?

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Great questions. Yes, heights can be zero. All values are non-negative integers. If the array is empty, return zero. The array length can be up to one hundred thousand.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Understood. So for the example two, one, five, six, two, three, I can see that bars at index two and three with heights five and six form a rectangle of area ten, using height five and width two. That's my target: find the maximum such area. I'll return a single integer. Let me start with a brute force approach.

sections.title: Brute Force Approach
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    subgraph BF["Brute Force: Check all pairs"]
        S1["i=0, j=0 to 5\nTrack min height"]:::blue
        S2["i=1, j=1 to 5\nTrack min height"]:::blue
        S3["..."]:::blue
        S4["i=2, j=2: area=5\ni=2, j=3: min=5, w=2, area=10"]:::blue
        S5["Max area found = 10"]:::blue
    end
    S1 --> S2 --> S3 --> S4 --> S5
    classDef blue fill:#60a5fa,color:#000

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: The simplest approach is to try every possible pair of left and right boundaries. For each pair, I find the minimum height among those bars and compute the area as minimum height times the width. I track the maximum area across all pairs.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Can you walk through that with our example?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Sure. Starting at index two with height five, I extend right to index three with height six. The minimum height is five, the width is two, so the area is ten. When I extend further to index four, the minimum drops to two and the area is two times three which is six. After checking all pairs, ten is the largest.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: We have two nested loops over n bars, so that gives us a time complexity of O of n-squared. Space is O of one since we only track the minimum and maximum. With up to one hundred thousand bars, this could be too slow. I think we can do better than that.

sections.title: Monotonic Stack Approach
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    subgraph MS["Monotonic Stack: heights = 2,1,5,6,2,3"]
        A["Push index 0, h=2
Stack: 0"]:::purple
        B["h=1 < 2: Pop 0
Area = 2*1 = 2
Push 1
Stack: 1"]:::purple
        C["Push 2, Push 3
Stack: 1,2,3"]:::purple
        D["h=2 < 6: Pop 3
Area = 6*1 = 6
Pop 2: Area = 5*2 = 10
Push 4
Stack: 1,4"]:::purple
        E["Push 5
Stack: 1,4,5"]:::purple
        F["End: Pop all remaining
Max area = 10"]:::purple
    end
    A --> B --> C --> D --> E --> F
    classDef purple fill:#a78bfa,color:#000

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: The key insight here is that we can use a monotonic stack. We maintain a stack of bar indices in increasing order of height. When we encounter a bar shorter than the top of the stack, we pop and calculate the area that bar could form as the shortest bar in a rectangle.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Walk me through the example using this stack approach.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: We push index zero with height two. At index one, height one is less than two, so we pop index zero. The area is two times one equals two. We push index one. Then we push indices two and three since heights five and six keep increasing. At index four, height two is less than six, so we pop index three. The width is one, area is six. We pop index two, height five. The width extends back to after index one, so width is two, area is ten. We push index four, then five. After the array ends, we pop remaining bars. The maximum area is ten.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: How do you determine the width when you pop a bar?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: When we pop a bar, the width extends from the current index on the right to one past the new stack top on the left. If the stack is empty after popping, the bar was the shortest seen so far, so the width is the current index. This lets us find the full span where each bar is the minimum height.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Each bar is pushed and popped at most once, so that gives us a time complexity of O of n. The stack holds at most n elements, so space complexity is also O of n. This handles one hundred thousand bars efficiently.

sections.title: Summary
sections.diagram:
graph LR
    subgraph Comparison["Approach Comparison"]
        BF["Brute Force\nTime: O of n-squared\nSpace: O of 1"]:::blue
        OPT["Monotonic Stack\nTime: O of n\nSpace: O of n"]:::purple
    end
    BF -->|"Optimize with stack"| OPT
    classDef blue fill:#60a5fa,color:#000
    classDef purple fill:#a78bfa,color:#000

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Great work. You went from an O of n-squared brute force to an elegant O of n solution using a monotonic stack. The stack approach is a classic pattern for problems where you need to find the nearest smaller element on both sides.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Thank you. The main takeaway is that a monotonic stack lets us efficiently track how far each bar can extend as the shortest in a rectangle. It avoids redundant comparisons by processing each bar exactly twice: once on push and once on pop.
